What Happens: Pick the game to solve: FHP (closest to NLH postflop), KuhnPoker, LeducPoker, etc.
Notes: FHP = 2-player fixed-limit holdem with 52 cards, 2 rounds, 3 community cards. For NLH postflop you'd need to restore nlhe_game.py from git history

What Happens: Pick solver algorithm. VRDeepPDCFRPlus is the best one (variance-reduced predictive deep CFR+)
Output: Solver class loaded dynamically via load_module()
Notes: Other options: OSDeepCFR, DREAM, NFSP, QPG, RPG -- but VRDeepPDCFRPlus is recommended

What Happens: Configure how long/hard to train: episodes, traversals per iteration, learning rate
Notes: num_traversals=10000 means 10K random game paths sampled per player per iteration

What Happens: Configure neural net architecture: layers, hidden units
Notes: Deeper/wider = more capacity but slower training. 3x64 works for small games

What Happens: Configure experience replay buffers for regret and policy data
Notes: Larger buffers = more diverse training data but more RAM. 150K regret + 1M policy fits in 48GB easily

What Happens: VRDeepPDCFR+ specific: alpha (temporal weighting), epsilon (exploration), gamma
Notes: alpha weighs recent vs old data. epsilon controls exploration mixing. These defaults are from the paper

What Happens: Choose compute device: cpu or mps (Apple GPU)
Output: PyTorch device for neural net ops
Notes: MPS available on your M4 Pro. If MPS errors occur, fall back to cpu

What Happens: Enable/disable logging, set eval frequency
Output: Log folder with data.csv + model checkpoints
Notes: Logs saved to logs/VRDeepPDCFRPlus/FHP/{run_id}/

What Happens: Run the training script with config
Code Entry Point: python scripts/run.py with configs/VRDeepPDCFRPlus.yaml game_name=FHP device=mps
Notes: Sacred framework handles config loading and experiment tracking

What Happens: run.py loads the solver class dynamically and creates solver instance
Output: Initialized solver with: game, 4 neural nets, 3 buffers, logger
Notes: Creates: 2 regret trainers (one per player), 1 average policy trainer, 1 baseline Q-value trainer

What Happens: Solver creates 4 types of neural nets: regret(x2 players), avg policy, baseline
Notes: Each regret trainer has 3 sub-networks: model, imm_model (immediate), target_model

What Happens: Calls evaluate() for baseline, then runs iterations until num_episodes reached
Notes: Each iteration processes both players. Evaluates every 3 iterations

What Happens: For each player: run num_traversals (10K) DFS traversals through random game paths
Input: Current game state + current network weights
Output: Regret samples added to ReservoirBuffer, policy samples added to policy buffer
Notes: External sampling MCCFR: at opponent nodes sample ONE action, at our nodes try ALL actions

What Happens: Train the regret network on collected regret samples (750 SGD steps)
Input: ReservoirBuffer with (infostate, regret_target, legal_mask, iteration) tuples
Notes: Loss combines immediate regrets + predicted long-term regrets with temporal weighting alpha=2.3

What Happens: Train Q-value baseline network for variance reduction
Input: CircularBuffer with (history, state, action, reward, legal_mask, next_state)
Notes: DQN-style training with target network. Reduces variance of regret estimates

What Happens: Train average policy network on accumulated policy data (5000 SGD steps)
Input: Policy buffer with (infostate, action_probs) from traversals
Notes: This is the FINAL strategy network used at inference time. Softmax output = action probabilities

What Happens: Compute exploitability of current strategy against best response
Output: Exploitability value (lower = closer to Nash equilibrium)
Notes: Logged to data.csv. Watch this number decrease over training. Target: <1% of pot

What Happens: Check data.csv or TensorBoard for exploitability trend
Output: Exploitability curve, regret losses, episode count
Notes: Stop training when exploitability plateaus or reaches acceptable level

What Happens: Logger automatically saves model state_dicts to .pkl files during training
Notes: Saved periodically based on logging schedule. Multiple checkpoints kept

What Happens: Can also manually save the key model after training
Notes: The average policy network is what you need for inference. Regret nets only needed to resume training

What Happens: For inference: save avg policy net. For resume training: save all 4 net types + buffers
Code Entry Point: torch.save({'policy': policy_sd, 'regret_0': r0_sd, 'regret_1': r1_sd, 'baseline': b_sd}, path)
Output: Single checkpoint file with all models
Notes: Also save the config YAML alongside for reproducibility

What Happens: Organize saved models in models/ directory
Notes: Keep game_name, network architecture params, and training metadata together

What Happens: Must recreate the same MLP architecture before loading weights
Output: Empty MLP network with correct shape
Notes: MUST match the architecture used during training exactly (same layers, hidden sizes)

What Happens: Load saved weights into the recreated network
Notes: Call model.eval() to disable dropout/batchnorm (if any). Set torch.no_grad() for inference

What Happens: Need the game object to convert user queries into infostate tensors
Notes: The game object provides: infostate_size, num_actions, legal_actions, state encoding

What Happens: Create a wrapper that takes a game state and returns action probabilities
Code Entry Point: def get_strategy(state): infostate = state.information_state_tensor(); logits = model(tensor); return softmax(logits * legal_mask)
Notes: This wrapper handles: tensor encoding, forward pass, legal action masking, regret matching or softmax

What Happens: Pick a Python web framework for serving the model
Notes: FastAPI gives you /docs endpoint for free. Flask is simpler alternative

What Happens: Define what the API accepts: game state description
Code Entry Point: POST /strategy with body: {player: 0, history: ['check', 'bet_100'], board: ['Ah','Kd','7s'], hand: ['Qs','Jh']}
Notes: For FHP: player position + action history + board cards + hole cards

What Happens: Convert API request into an OpenSpiel game state
Code Entry Point: game.new_initial_state() -> replay action history to reach current state
Output: OpenSpiel State object at the queried decision point
Notes: Must map human-readable actions (check/bet/fold) to OpenSpiel action IDs

What Happens: Run the loaded model on the reconstructed state
Code Entry Point: with torch.no_grad(): logits = model(infostate_tensor); strategy = regret_match_or_softmax(logits, legal_mask)
Notes: ~1ms on MPS, ~10ms on CPU per query

What Happens: Convert raw model output to human-readable strategy
Code Entry Point: Map action indices to names, pair with probabilities, return JSON
Notes: Filter to legal actions only. Include EV estimates if available

What Happens: Start the FastAPI server
Notes: Model loaded once at startup, kept in memory for fast inference

What Happens: Client sends POST request to the API
Notes: Can also use Python requests, JavaScript fetch, or the /docs Swagger UI

What Happens: Read the action probabilities returned
Output: Human-readable GTO strategy for that spot
Notes: Probabilities sum to 1.0. Higher prob = preferred action. Mixed strategy = randomize according to probs

What Happens: Query ALL hands at one decision point to see full range strategy
Code Entry Point: POST /range with body: {player: 0, history: ['check'], board: ['Ah','Kd','7s']} -- loops over all 1326 combos
Output: Full range: {hand: strategy} for all possible holdings
Notes: This gives you the GTO range chart similar to PioSOLVER output. ~1-2 seconds for all 1326 combos

What Happens: Validate model accuracy by comparing to known solver output (if available)
Code Entry Point: Compare model.action_probabilities(state) vs known_solver_strategy[state] across sample of states
Output: Accuracy metrics: avg KL divergence, max strategy error per action
Notes: For FHP: can compute exact Nash and compare. For NLH: compare against PioSOLVER exports if available
